```{r q3}
ck    <- tab("q3_choose_k.csv")
nul   <- tab("q3_null_test.csv")
stab  <- tab("q3_stability.csv")
tests <- tab("q3_tests.csv")
mix   <- tab("q3_type_mix.csv")
types <- tab("q3_types.csv")
rbt   <- tab("q3_residual_by_type.csv")
k     <- nul$k_chosen
sil_k <- ck$silhouette[ck$k == k]; sil_3 <- ck$silhouette[ck$k == 3]
ta    <- tests[grepl("H0\\(a\\)", tests$hypothesis), ]
tb    <- tests[grepl("H0\\(b\\)", tests$hypothesis), ]
share <- function(m, cl) mix$share[mix$maturity == m & mix$cluster == cl]
low   <- types$cluster[grepl("^Low", types$name)]
high  <- types$cluster[grepl("^High", types$name)]
sc    <- readRDS(file.path(ROOT, "data", "processed", "score_subzone.rds")) %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% filter(residential)
pc1   <- summary(prcomp(scale(sc[paste0("score_", names(CAT_LAB))])))$importance[2, 1]
prof  <- tab("q3_profiles.csv") %>% filter(cluster == low)
mat_ext <- readr::read_csv(file.path(ROOT, "data", "external", "town_maturity.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
# Blocks that carry a town label are the units H0(a) permutes.
n_lab_blocks <- proc("q1_blocks.csv") %>%
  left_join(proc("census2020_subzone.csv") %>% select(subzone_c, pln_area_n), by = "subzone_c") %>%
  left_join(mat_ext %>% select(pln_area_n, maturity), by = "pln_area_n") %>%
  filter(maturity %in% c("mature", "non-mature")) %>% distinct(block_id) %>% nrow()
# What H0(a) leaves out: the Central Area (mature in HDB's list, excluded by
# design), private Tanglin and non-town areas.
res_pa <- proc("residential_set.csv") %>% filter(residential) %>% select(subzone_c) %>%
  left_join(proc("census2020_subzone.csv") %>% select(subzone_c, pln_area_n, pop, dw_hdb, dw_total), by = "subzone_c") %>%
  left_join(mat_ext %>% select(pln_area_n, maturity, note), by = "pln_area_n") %>%
  mutate(central = maturity == "excluded" & grepl("Central Area", note))
excl <- res_pa %>% filter(maturity == "excluded")
hdb_central <- res_pa %>% filter(central) %>% group_by(pln_area_n) %>%
  summarise(hdb = sum(dw_hdb) / sum(dw_total), .groups = "drop") %>% filter(hdb > 0.5) %>%
  pull(pln_area_n) %>% tolower() %>% tools::toTitleCase()
hh_comp <- proc("q1_lisa.csv") %>% filter(variable == "score", cluster == "High-High")
```

# Q3: What kinds of neighbourhood exist?

**H₀(a)**: the mix of neighbourhood types is the same in mature and non-mature towns. **H₀(b)**: type membership is unrelated to Q2's residuals.

**Method.** We clustered the `r sum(stab$n_subzones)` residential subzones with k-means [@hartigan1979], using their six category scores as z-scores so each category weighs equally. The lectures used k-means only to bin map colours. The number of groups k is chosen by the highest mean silhouette, a measure of how much better each subzone fits its own group than the next one [@rousseeuw1987]. On simulated data with three planted groups, the same code recovers exactly three.

**No evidence of discrete types.** The silhouette rule picks k = `r k` (`r num(sil_k, 2)`, against `r num(sil_3, 2)` at k = 3; Figure 5). But silhouette always picks some k ≥ 2, even in data with no groups. We therefore re-ran the same rule on `r nul$n_null` simulated datasets that have the real scores' correlations but no groups at all (a no-cluster null in the spirit of the gap statistic [@tibshirani2001], but keeping the scores' correlations; the same logic as Lecture 7's simulation envelope). The real data separate no better than these structureless clouds:

- observed silhouette `r num(nul$observed_max_silhouette, 3)`;
- null mean `r num(nul$null_mean, 3)`, 95th percentile `r num(nul$null_q95, 3)`;
- p = `r num(nul$p_value, 2)`.

The six scores move together along one general-access axis: a principal component analysis, which finds the single direction that captures most of their variation [@james2021], puts `r pct(pc1, 0)` of it on the first component. The data give no evidence that k = `r k` is more than a cut through that axis. Both halves are reproducible: in a spatial block bootstrap [@kunsch1989; @hennig2007] that resamples Q1's planning-area blocks 200 times, their mean Jaccard overlap (subzones in both the original and the resampled group, divided by subzones in either) is `r num(min(stab$mean_jaccard), 2)`–`r num(max(stab$mean_jaccard), 2)`, well above the 0.75 stability bar. A cut through a continuum is also stable, though, so this confirms a repeatable split, not distinct types. We call the halves the **low-access end** (`r types$n_subzones[types$cluster == low]` subzones, every category `r num(-max(prof$mean_z), 1)`–`r num(-min(prof$mean_z), 1)` SD below average) and the **high-access end** (`r types$n_subzones[types$cluster == high]`). Their profiles differ in level, not in mix (Figures 6 and 7).

```{r fig-k, fig.cap = "Figure 5. Choosing k: within-cluster sum of squares and mean silhouette.", out.width = "90%"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("q3_choose_k.png"))
```

```{r fig-profiles, fig.cap = "Figure 6. Mean z-score per category for the two ends of the access gradient.", out.width = "80%"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("q3_profiles.png"))
```

```{r fig-types-map, fig.cap = "Figure 7. The two ends of the access gradient across Singapore.", out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("q3_types_map.png"))
```

**H₀(a): not rejected.** The low-access end holds `r pct(share("mature", low))` of mature-town subzones and `r pct(share("non-mature", low))` of non-mature ones, a gap of `r num(100 * abs(share("mature", low) - share("non-mature", low)), 1)` points. Neighbouring subzones are not independent, so the textbook χ² p-value would be too small. Instead, town labels were permuted between whole blocks (the label is set by planning area, so shuffling within a block would change nothing). The statistic is Pearson's χ² for the table of type by town group, which grows as the two mixes diverge [@rice2007]. The gap is within chance (χ² = `r num(ta$observed, 2)`, p = `r num(ta$p_value, 2)`) [@good2005]. But only `r n_lab_blocks` labelled blocks can be exchanged, so the test has little power: this is no evidence of a difference, not evidence of equal mixes. HDB counts the Central Area as a mature estate, but we leave its planning areas out by design, as we do largely private Tanglin and a few non-town areas: `r nrow(excl)` residential subzones with `r pct(sum(excl$pop) / sum(res_pa$pop), 0)` of residents. Most Central Area subzones are private or commercial, though `r paste(hdb_central, collapse = " and ")` hold HDB estates. The exclusion matters for reading the result: the Central Area holds `r sum(hh_comp$subzone_c %in% res_pa$subzone_c[res_pa$central])` of the composite's `r nrow(hh_comp)` hot-spot subzones from Q1, so H₀(a) compares the heartland towns, not the city centre with the rest.

**H₀(b): rejected, but the test cannot discriminate.** Q2's residuals were permuted within blocks. The low-access end averages `r num(abs(rbt$mean_residual[rbt$cluster == low]), 1)` points below what the five Q2 predictors imply, and the high-access end `r num(rbt$mean_residual[rbt$cluster == high], 1)` above (F = `r num(tb$observed, 1)`, the one-way analysis-of-variance ratio of spread between the groups' mean residuals to spread within them [@rice2007]; p ≤ `r num(1 / (tb$n_perm + 1), 3)`, the permutation floor). But the groups are cut by score level, and the residual is the score minus its prediction. Whenever the model leaves anything unexplained, the low group must get negative residuals, so this test rejects by construction. We report the residual means as a description only.
